01 WHAT'S THE ISSUE?

Three everyday expressions.
Three questions worth asking.

Explore how collective pronouns, job labels and honorifics can carry assumptions in some settings. Click a phrase to see what changes when context comes first.

GENERIC MASCULINE

“Neutral” on the page?

In written Chinese, 他 can look masculine even when 他们 is intended to refer to a mixed group. Whether this creates a male-default interpretation depends on usage, audience and context.

THE QUESTION: Could we name the audience directly?

These examples invite reflection—not a universal ban on words.

INSTEAD OF SAYING
等他们到了就开始。
“We’ll start when they arrive.”
CONSIDER SAYING
等大家到了就开始。
“We’ll start when everyone arrives.”
02 WHY IT MATTERS

Language does more than describe. It frames.

The project brings sociolinguistic ideas into an everyday public-communication setting.

01 / ↗

Default assumptions

A form intended to include everyone may still prompt a narrower mental image for some readers. Research on generic masculine forms motivates this question, though findings differ across languages and contexts.

02 / ✳

Unnecessary marking

Calling someone a “female driver” when gender is irrelevant can shift attention from the professional role to a marked identity. Why specify gender here, but not elsewhere?

03 / ◎

Audience & context

No single expression works everywhere. A clear message considers who is listening, why the message is being delivered, and which details actually help.

✳

We're not banning words. We're making room for more thoughtful choices.

THE DO–SAY TOOLKIT

Role first.
Context always.

Small shifts can move attention back to the people, roles and messages that matter.

Instead of他们
generic mixed group
→
Try saying大家 / 各位
everyone / all
Instead of女司机
female driver
→
Try saying司机
driver
Instead of“先生”
gendered praise
→
Try saying姓名 / 职业头衔
name / role title

Guiding principle: Add gender when it genuinely informs the message. Interpret honorifics with cultural and situational care.

04 BEHIND THE RESEARCH

From linguistic theory
to public conversation.

This interactive project grows from an original bilingual public communication poster and accompanying academic exegesis.

A visual homage, not a replica.

The blue-and-yellow campaign look draws on the assertive graphic language of J. Howard Miller's 1943 We Can Do It! poster.

Making an academic question public.

The original LING8013 public communication piece was designed for bilingual university audiences who write announcements, meeting openers and other messages in Chinese.

Rather than treating inclusive language as a rigid word-replacement rule, the project uses familiar examples and practical alternatives to encourage audience-aware choices.

Original formatBilingual A3 poster + exegesis
AudienceANU bilingual student community
Research lensGeneric masculine · markedness
Design lensAudience design · clarity
01
Identify familiar expressions

Three recurring patterns: 他们, gender-first job labels and asymmetric honorific usage.

02
Connect evidence to audience needs

Bring work on language ideology, markedness and audience design into a short, accessible explanation.

03
Turn critique into action

Build a bilingual instead-of / try-saying toolkit, then extend it into an interactive web experience.

Research boundary: The poster's effects were not experimentally evaluated. Findings from other languages should not be treated as direct proof of how every Mandarin speaker interprets these expressions. Honorific usage is highly context-specific.
